community-s8c/u1.input:
The vaccination point belongs here. It's one of the values that would decide whether I could raise children inside a community at all. I'm not trying to design a village for everyone. A community needs enough agreement on children's health that parents can actually trust one another.

The grown child's review matters more than founders usually want it to. Adults can describe their intentions forever. The person who lived through the system may eventually describe something else.
community-s8c/u1.A:
I'd say the vaccination thing is a definite should have for where I'd want to bring up children. However, I'm not trying to create a village for all people, just for a community that shares enough in common to trust each other with the health of their children.

Interestingly, as a child of mine is now grown, I think he would be much more useful in this review that the adults setting up the system. The adults can only talk about what they intend to do.
community-s8c/u1.B:
I would make this a vaccination point in any community I join. It would play into the decision of whether or not it would be safe to raise kids in that community. I think that is essential to any community that has a set of agreed upon values. It is not for everyone but it is for some. A communities health is too important to take chances on that issue.

I think the review from one of the grown children will be far more revealing than the words of the founders. Time will tell what really happened. I only know what adults say now that they no longer are affected by the system.

community-s8c/u2.input:
A friend who reviewed this draft grew up in a Christian commune in Colorado, where her father was a pastor. She calls her childhood “a treasure and a burden.” The treasure was belonging, and having everybody care for everybody. The burden was a strict religious life she never chose.

That sentence is more useful than another promotional video of smiling children carrying vegetables.
community-s8c/u2.A:
In a previous draft of this post, a friend who grew up in a Christian commune out in Colorado with her pastor dad described her experience growing up there as a treasure and a burden. A treasure because she was always part of a community where everybody took care of everybody. A burden because she was forced to live a very religious life.

That’s more useful than another video showing kids smiling and carrying vegetables.
community-s8c/u2.B:
In her review of this draft, a friend of mind who grew up in a Christian commune in Colorado (her dad was a pastor) said her experience was “a treasure and a burden.” A treasure because she knew she belonged, and everybody cared for everybody. A burden because she was expected to live a strict religious life she had no say in.

Wow. This is so much better than watching yet another promo video of kids carrying vegetables and smiling.

community-s8c/u3.input:
My position is that mothers raise their own children, inside a community where the care really is shared. The village can take on meals, supervision, teaching, protection, play, and a lot of the fathering. It should never take a child away from the mother in the name of liberating her.

Jean Liedloff's The Continuum Concept is one of the biggest reasons I think community matters for children. Her account of the Ye'kuana is one outsider's interpretation, and she may idealize what she saw. But the picture is still powerful. Babies are carried inside ordinary adult life. Children are surrounded by people of several ages, and they learn by taking part. And one exhausted parent isn't expected to become the child's whole social world. A nuclear household can imitate pieces of this. A real village can make it normal.
community-s8c/u3.A:
I’m in the camp that says that the moms should raise the kids, but that doesn’t mean that it should all be on the moms, it should be on the whole village. The village should help the moms with meals, supervision, teaching, protection, playing, fathering, etc., but not take the kids from the moms to “liberate” the moms.

One great book on the importance of community to children is The Continuum Concept by Jean Liedloff. While it is through the lens of someone not of the Ye’kuana tribe, and it may even be a bit idealized, it is great. The babies are carried, included in all of the adult’s activities, there are lots of different aged people around the kids, the kids learn through inclusion, and there isn’t a worn-out parent that is the only social interaction the kids have. While some of this can be done by a nuclear household, it is so much better when the whole village is there.
community-s8c/u3.B:
It's pretty clear from the way I'm writing that I think mothers should raise their kids. But, it also is pretty clear that I think they should do it within the context of a community that "helps". Not to take the kids, mind, but to help with the meals, supervision, teaching, protection, playing, fathering, etc. It's not to "liberate" the mother from her children, that's for sure.

One of the books I've learned the most from about how kids need and benefit from community is Jean Liedloff's Continuum Concept. She writes about her time with the Ye'kuana tribe, and while it is her interpretation (and she tends to idealize them a bit in my opinion) it is a great book. She talks about how the babies are carried with them and involved in the adult activities, how the kids are surrounded by several age groups at all times, how they learn, and how it doesn't fall on one tired parent to be their whole social world. While some of this can be mimicked to a degree in a nuclear household situation, it's far better in a village.

community-s8c/u4.input:
Experiments where children sleep and live apart from their parents need special caution. Research on Israeli kibbutzim found that communal sleeping eventually ended, through a mix of developmental findings, parents' preferences and social change. High-quality group care, and several loving adults, can be good for children. Replacing a secure attachment to the parents is a different matter.

Tamera's Children's Place deserves to be studied directly, not caricatured. My own bias is still toward systems that widen a child's circle without making the bond between parent and child ideologically inconvenient.
community-s8c/u4.A:
Experiments of that magnitude, where children not only sleep, but also live away from their parents, should be conducted with extra caution and there are good reasons to why the communistic way of letting kids sleep apart from their parents was finally abolished in Israeli kibbutzim (due to a combination of developmental findings, parental preference and social change). While there is nothing wrong with kids being with other people, enjoying high quality group care and being loved by a handful of people, none of that can nor should replace secure attachment to their parents.

That being said, it is worth taking a look at what they do at the Children's Place at Tamera. Personally, the way things are done there doesn't seem as "problematic" to be (but that's coming from someone who is biased towards systems that don't see parental bonding as an "ideological issue" and are willing to open up the circles around kids)
community-s8c/u4.B:
Yes, these kind of experiments should be treated with extra caution. Even on the Kibbutzim in Israel where the children slept and eventually lived apart from the parents the practice has been discontinued after many years due to a combination of research findings, parental preferences and social change. Group living can be good for children - in very good conditions, and it can be very good for a child to have contact with several different loving adults - but it does not substitute for a secure attachment to the parents.

But Tamera can of course be studied in their Childrens Place. It is just that, like every person, i come with a bias for these kind of systems, and i am more in favor of those systems that do not make parent-child bonding ideologically unfavorable.

community-s8c/u5.input:
Children also need some territory that belongs to them. Places where they can build their own society of children, make up games, sort out ordinary disputes, and get some freedom from constant adult management.

I got a taste of that at a Unitarian youth camp, and it's still one of the freest memories I have. ZEGG's Kinderhaus works from a similar idea. The adults hold the outer safety, and the children still get a world of their own.
community-s8c/u5.A:
And kids need their own territory, their own space to create their own society in, play their own games and even fight their own fights without always beeing under the management of adults.

One of the freest places I ever was was a youth camp of the Unitarian church, by the way. ZEGG tries to do something similar with their „Kinderhaus“, where the adults only hold the outside secure and safe and the kids create their own world.
community-s8c/u5.B:
Children need their own place and territory, where they can construct their own, children's society - without the involvement of adults. The kids invent their own games and play together.

I remember that from my time in a youth camp of the Unitarian Church - it was one of the freest things I have experienced in my life. In the ZEGG Kinderhaus, the adults take care of safety on the outside - but the kids construct their own world.

community-s8c/u6.input:
This can be badly misunderstood, so the safeguards have to be spelled out. A children's territory can't turn into a place where adults stop paying attention. Or where older kids dominate younger ones without anyone noticing. Or where secrecy gets treated as independence.

I also reject the suburban panic that treats every warm relationship between a child and an unrelated adult as suspicious. Children do well with lots of adults around who know them and enjoy them, who notice when something changes, and who will act when something's wrong. Fear can destroy that gift without actually preventing abuse.
community-s8c/u6.A:
It occurred to me that this could be taken in a bad way, so let me add a few safegaurds here. This is not meant to allow a space where adults are not paying attention. It is not meant to allow older kids to run the show with younger kids. It is not meant to allow kids to be secret in a bad way.

Finally, I don't want people to think I'm one of those suburbanites who thinks it's odd for a child to have a positive relationship with an adult who is not related to them. I think it's great for kids to have tons of positive relationships with adults. But I think that when those adults act on their fears, they destroy something good for kids.
community-s8c/u6.B:
This would have to be very carefully guarded, because it could so easily be misused. No children's territory could not become a place where grownups do not pay attention, where older kids run over the younger ones, or where the kids feel they must keep secrets from the grownups.

I don't buy the suburban paranoia that says that children should not have warm relationships with a lot of grownups who are not related to them. It is a wonderful thing for a child to know and be known by many grownups who enjoy them and who would be alert to and act upon any kind of problem that might arise. Paranoia will not keep kids safe.

community-s8c/u7.input:
The protection has several parts:

Give children real agency. Their “no” matters. No adult is entitled to a child's affection, physical contact, obedience beyond what legitimate safety requires, or private access.

Make a no-secrets rule. No adult asks a child to hide a gift, a game, a touch, a conversation, or a relationship from the child's mother or another trusted adult. A surprise has a date when it ends. Secrets meant to isolate the child are forbidden.
community-s8c/u7.A:
Other things it includes are:

Children can say “No!” to anything they want to, and no grown-up has a right to a child’s love, body, obedience, or access. (Obedience for legitimate safety reasons is not considered here.)

No grown-up may ever ask a child to keep a secret from his mother or other trusted adults. No grown-up may ever give a child a gift, play a game, touch, talk to, or have a relationship with the child that the child must keep secret from his mother or other trusted adults.
community-s8c/u7.B:
There are a few things here.

One of them is to teach the kids to have a sense of ownership of themselves and that “no” is a word they can use and adults are not entitled to their affection or physical contact with them or access to them. There are some things adults can say “yes” to for the kids because they have legitimate authority in some situations, but these are very limited.

Another thing is the rule of no secrets. There are many ways of enforcing this but the easiest is to make it clear no adult is allowed to ask the kids to not tell their mother or whoever, about anything that adult does for them, with them, anything at all.

community-s8c/u8.input:
Teach truthfulness before there's a crisis. Children should understand that their words carry power, and that adults will take them seriously. That teaching must never turn into interrogation, into punishing a child for being unsure, or into a reason to dismiss what a child reports. A scared or confused child may tell the story imperfectly and still need protecting.

Hear the child even when the accused person is someone people love. This is where communities fail, because that adult may be charismatic, useful, wealthy, spiritually important, or everybody's friend. Decide how you'll respond before anyone's face is attached to it. Immediate safety comes first. The investigation has to be competent and fair. And nobody's status buys silence.
community-s8c/u8.A:
Third, you’ve already taken the time to teach your kids to tell the truth, without making it a toxic thing where they are punished for not being able to accurately answer a question, or believing that they won’t be believed. They know that what they say is powerful and will be taken seriously. (This is another thing to work on now, not when you’re in the middle of a situation where a scared kid is trying to tell you that she needs to be protected.)

Fourth, you will believe her/him even if the accused is someone you really love. This is where a lot of people and communities fall down. The accused is someone charismatic, valuable, rich, spiritually important, a good friend, etc. You’ve already discussed what you are going to do in the immediate moment to ensure safety, who will investigate the matter competently and fairly, and what you will do to ensure that it isn’t hushed up for the protection of the perpetrator.
community-s8c/u8.B:
It will be useful to teach your children to be truthful, without making them feel like they’ll be in trouble for not remembering things precisely, or for reporting things that you may wish were not true.

And it will be useful to decide what you’ll do if you think that a child is telling the truth about something — especially if the accused is someone you love. That’s the place where communities are weakest, because usually the adult is someone charming or valuable or wealthy or important or friendly. But in advance, think through what you need to do to make sure that the child is safe immediately, that the investigation is done competently and fairly, and that the issue is not covered up.

community-s8c/u9.input: Keep relationships, and a way to report, outside the community. Grandparents, cousins, local friends, teachers and other trusted adults give children perspective, and somewhere to speak. At least one trusted adult, advocate or reporting route should be reachable without going through the community's leadership. In 1984, Vermont authorities seized 112 children in the Island Pond raid, and the court gave them back after it rejected the state's blanket request. State intervention can fail spectacularly. A community that closes itself off completely can fail too. Children need more than one world.
community-s8c/u9.A: Were it possible, it would be a good idea to ensure that relationships and reporting mechanisms exist outside the community (grandparents, cousins, local friends, teachers, etc.) so that there is always at least one trusted adult / advocate / reporting mechanism that doesn’t go directly to the community leadership. However, this won’t always be possible, and, as the 1984 Island Pond Raid showed, state intervention is not always effective. In that case, Vermont authorities seized 112 children, only to have a court rule against the blanket state request and order their return.
community-s8c/u9.B: The first is to not cut off all relations to the outside world. Children should have relationships with people outside the community, such as grandparents, cousins, friends from down the street, or even teachers. They need to know that there is someone they can go to, if something should happen. At least one trusted adult, advocate, or way to report abuse should be outside of the direct control of the community leadership. Why? Because governments can be incompetent. In 1984, the government of Vermont seized 112 children from their homes in a raid on Island Pond, and a court had to return them after rejecting the state’s request to take them all at once.

community-s8c/u10.input: I also searched the research corpus for a well-documented case, in an intentional community, of a child who stayed seriously dangerous to other people, where the record follows the whole sequence: the conduct, the assessment, the intervention, the review, and what happened afterwards. I didn't find one. That may be because the records are private, or because cases were sent elsewhere. But it means I can't claim that communities already know how to handle the hardest version on their own. The child, the family and the people at risk all need access to competent help and review that the home community doesn't control.
community-s8c/u10.A: I have done my best to search the research corpus for any case that details a child, in an intentional community context, that maintained a serious level of danger to others, and where the full sequence of events, assessment, intervention, review and follow up are described. No such case has been forthcoming. This may be, of course, due to the issues being dealt with in private, or by sending the problem elsewhere. In either case, it seems to me that the child and the family should have access to a competent resource for help and review that is outside of the control of the home community.
community-s8c/u10.B: Also, I have done some searching in my own corpus of research, and I don't have any examples of long-term seriously dangerous-to-others children in intentional communities. Maybe the information is out there and I'm not seeing it because it's private. Or maybe they turned over to other communities. Either way, it sounds like access to competent help, not controlled by the home community, would be useful for the child, family, and potentially dangerous people.

community-s8c/u11.input:
Amish young people make an adult choice about whether to join the church, and roughly 85 percent or more eventually do. The popular caricature of Rumspringa as a free-for-all that every teenager goes through is exaggerated. But adult baptism still matters, because it makes belonging a commitment instead of a fact imposed at birth.

If a community's children never leave, it can't know whether they'd come back freely. Let them study, travel and make friends. Let them run into other ways of life, and disagree with the founders without being treated as traitors.
community-s8c/u11.A:
A big difference between the Amish and some cultish groups is that the Amish allow their youth to decide for themselves when they come of age whether or not to join the church. Sure, 85% or more of them do choose to join, and the Rumspringa thing is blown out of proportion in popular culture, but the fact that they are baptized as adults and not as infants is significant.

If all the children stay, then how would they know if the children would return if allowed to leave? Allow the children to study, travel, and make friends. Allow them to denounce the ways of the founders.
community-s8c/u11.B:
First of all, the Amish only join their church when they are adults and about 85% (or is it more?) do join. Secondly, the Rumspringa isn't really as big of a thing as it's cracked up to be. And the whole point of being bapitised as an adult is that it HAS to be a choice.

If they don't let the children go, they'll never know if they'd come back. Let them study, let them travel, let them make friends, let them disagree with whatever the founder said.

community-s8c/u12.input: Every childhood narrows the future. Most ordinary families don't hand an eighteen-year-old a pile of money to go explore the world. They try to get them ready for some next step that can actually work. A poor or money-free community may have even less cash to offer, and food, medical care and basic survival may rightly come first.
community-s8c/u12.A: As someone that grew up in a normal community, that was neither rich nor extremely poor, not having money at all is going to limit what a kid can do. If someone grew up poor, it's not likely that at age 18 they're going to get some money from their parents to go travel the world. It's more likely that their parents want them to go to the next step, wherever that may be. Food, medical care, and other simple things are going to be a priority in a community without money.
community-s8c/u12.B: It depends on the life they grew up in, too. Unless they come from a really rich family, it's unlikely that they would just give their kid a ton of money at 18 and say, "Go see the world." Most families, even those in a poor or money-less community, would be more interested in getting their child ready for something that's going to actually work. Being able to eat and take care of themselves and their medical needs would be a top priority for those families.

community-s8c/u13.input: The realistic standard isn't unlimited freedom. It's that leaving shouldn't be made artificially impossible. If children grow up without using money, they especially need to know enough about the money world outside not to be helpless in it: jobs, rent, contracts, banking, scams, ID, transportation, and how to ask for help. They need skills and an education they can take with them, relationships outside the community, access to their own records and documents, and at least one plausible next path, whether that's school, an apprenticeship, work, family or another community. If the community can offer temporary housing, help with travel, tools, or a small reserve for the transition, great. If it can't, it can still avoid punishing anyone for leaving, or holding back the knowledge and the records a young adult needs to function somewhere else. No upbringing gives perfect freedom. The point isn't to erase path dependence. It's to not turn belonging into a trap.
community-s8c/u13.A: What if, instead of some unrealistic standard, the standard is not making leaving impossible? In the case of children who have not used money at all, a part of being ready to leave should include education about the money world, so that they know how to get a job, or how to pay rent, or how contracts work, or how to open a bank account, or how to not get scammed, or how to get ID, or how to get around, or how to get help, etc. Other things that could be done include helping them get useful skills and education that are valuable outside the community, allowing them to build relationships with people outside the community, allowing them to have records and documents that they can take with them when they leave, helping them have at least one place to go when they leave (school, apprenticeship, job, family, community, etc), or providing them with resources to help them get set up when they leave (housing, transportation, tools, etc). If the community doesn't want to provide any of those, at least they could make sure that they are not punishing people for leaving, and not withholding information or records from them. No way of raising children creates total freedom for them to do whatever they want, due to path dependence, but at least the community could try to not trap them.
community-s8c/u13.B: What would be realistic is a standard that didn't make it impossible for people to leave a group if they wanted to. Especially for kids who grew up without money at all, it would be nice for them to at least have a basic knowledge of how the outside money-world works, some skills, some education, some connections with people outside the community, access to all their records and other documents, and at least one place they can go when they leave (ideally also some kind of financial, material, or lodging support to ease the transition, but even if the community can't support that, they can at least not make leaving actively hard by holding back the above items). It's not really possible to make someone's options not path-dependent, but it is possible to avoid actively trapping people.

community-s8c/u14.input:
Some of them may leave for good. Others may start communities with different values, instead of waiting decades to inherit the original one. Parents may feel that as a loss, even when it's the movement evolving.

Couples who share a home, a culture and a bed still split over screens, vaccines, schooling, religion, food, discipline and medical care. Now multiply that by twenty adults with twenty childhoods.

Goodwill doesn't answer those questions once a child is already living inside the disagreement. A community needs enough shared principles about raising children to offer coherence, and enough room left for parents to still be parents.
community-s8c/u14.A:
The reality is a lot of them might leave. Or they'll start their own communities with the values they want instead of waiting to inherit them someday. And that will feel like a loss too, for their parents.

People who live together, who share culture and even beds, disagree about screens and vaccines and schooling and religion and food and discipline and medicine. Why would 20 people with 20 different childhoods be any different?

Good will isn't enough, once there are children in the middle. Communities need a certain level of shared principles about how to raise children that also allows people to be parents.
community-s8c/u14.B:
It is entirely possible that some will leave, and some may start their own communities with different values. This may feel like a loss to some parents, but hopefully will be understood as the movement evolving.

Even cohabitating couples sharing a bed and a culture can disagree about screens, vaccines, schooling, religion, food, discipline, medical care, and more. This is even more likely to be true when 20 different adults with 20 different childhoods come together.

Goodwill alone will not resolve all conflicts, so it will be important to find a balance between establishing a common set of principles around children and allowing the parents to be the parents.

community-s8d/u1.A: As far as presenting a position, here it is: Mothers should raise their children but in a context where the ‘village’ does raise the children by providing many of the things they need other than a mother. The village does not “take” the child away from the mother to ‘liberate’ her but rather helps her by providing meals, supervision, teaching, protection, play, fathering, etc.
community-s8d/u1.B: To clarify, the line of thought behind this, is that women should raise their OWN children. The village would be there to raise them WITH that mother, in her community. The village helping to meal prep, to watch, to teach, to protect, to play with, and yes, even to father that child. Not to take the child FROM that mother in an effort to 'liberate' her from the burden of mothering, that is ridiculous.

Children are surrounded by people of several ages, and they learn by taking part. And one exhausted parent isn't expected to become the child's whole social world. A nuclear household can imitate pieces of this. A real village can make it normal.
community-s8d/u2.A: Part of what draws me to this idea is what Jean Liedloff talks about in The Continuum Concept. Keep in mind that this is an outsider's view on the Ye'kuana, and she may be idealizing them to a certain extent, but she notes that they carry their babies with them wherever they go and integrate them into daily life, that children interact with multiple age groups, and that children learn by participating in daily life rather than having an exhausted parent try to provide their entire social life. While it's possible to try to recreate some of this in a nuclear household setting, it could just as easily (or more easily) be part of normal life in a village.
community-s8d/u2.B: One of the reasons I think the idea of creating a community for children is so important has to do with Jean Liedloff and The Continuum Concept. Although her experience and descriptions of the Ye'kuana tribe are obviously colored through the filter of her own mind and perhaps even a bit romanticized, there are many aspects of the way she describes the Ye'kuana raising their children that I think are healthy and beneficial. Babies are included in the adult world from the moment they are born. Children are surrounded by a variety of ages all the time. Children learn by doing. And, perhaps most importantly for me, it takes the burden off of any one individual (usually the mother) to be the sole social force in a child's life. While it's possible for a nuclear household to try and imitate these aspects to some extent, it would be far better if an entire village were functioning in this way.

This is where communities fail, because that adult may be charismatic, useful, wealthy, spiritually important, or everybody's friend. Decide how you'll respond before anyone's face is attached to it. Immediate safety comes first. The investigation has to be competent and fair. And nobody's status buys silence.

Be clear in your own mind in advance as to what you will do when you hear of an allegation. Put everyone in immediate safety. See that a competent and fair investigation is done. Don’t allow anyone to hide behind the protection of status in the community.
community-s8d/u6.B: Can you hear the child when he tells you that someone you love has hurt him? This is where communities fail. The adult may be charismatic. Or helpful. Or rich. Or a spiritual leader. Or simply everybody's friend. How will you react in advance? First, protect the child's safety. Then ensure a competent and fair investigation. Not everybody gets to buy silence.

community-s8d/u7.input: Keep relationships, and a way to report, outside the community. Grandparents, cousins, local friends, teachers and other trusted adults give children perspective, and somewhere to speak. At least one trusted adult, advocate or reporting route should be reachable without going through the community's leadership. In 1984, Vermont authorities seized 112 children in the Island Pond raid, and the court gave them back after it rejected the state's blanket request. State intervention can fail spectacularly. A community that closes itself off completely can fail too. Children need more than one world.
community-s8d/u7.A: Relationships with, and ways of reporting to, people outside the community must be allowed. Grandparents, cousins, friends in nearby towns, schoolteachers, and others can provide important context and avenues for reporting wrongdoing. Every adult should have at least one trusted adult, advocate, or reporting avenue, preferably outside the chain of command of the community leadership. In 1984, authorities in Vermont seized 112 children in a dramatic action at Island Pond, but a court threw out the state’s blanket request to take custody of the children.
community-s8d/u7.B: The kids need to be plugged in to the outside world a bit. It is important for them to have relationships and to be able to talk to people outside the community. They should have at least one trusted adult or advocate who can help them report abuse if needed and who is not part of the community leadership. The state can be awful at this stuff. In 1984 they seized 112 kids in Island Pond, Vermont but a court rejected their request en masse. But they also can't be totally cut off.

community-s8d/u8.input: I also searched the research corpus for a well-documented case, in an intentional community, of a child who stayed seriously dangerous to other people, where the record follows the whole sequence: the conduct, the assessment, the intervention, the review, and what happened afterwards. I didn't find one. That may be because the records are private, or because cases were sent elsewhere. But it means I can't claim that communities already know how to handle the hardest version on their own. The child, the family and the people at risk all need access to competent help and review that the home community doesn't control.
community-s8d/u8.A: Also, I've looked for good documentation of what actually happened in a real case of a child in an intentional community who continued to be seriously dangerous to other people. I haven't been able to find a case where enough of the sequence of events, assessment, intervention, and review is described. It may exist but be private, or it may be that they all ended up referring such cases somewhere. In any case, it seems to me that the child, the family, and potential victims all deserve access to competent help and review that is not under the control of the home community.
community-s8d/u8.B: On a quick search of my research corpus I found no record of a specific case within an intentional community of a child who remained dangerously inclined towards others, and for which there is a record of the full sequence of events, assessments and interventions, and of subsequent review. That may be because these matters are private, or it may be because such cases are referred elsewhere; in any case it seems essential that the child and family should have access to competent help and review that is not under the control of their home community.

community-s8d/u9.input: Amish young people make an adult choice about whether to join the church, and roughly 85 percent or more eventually do. The popular caricature of Rumspringa as a free-for-all that every teenager goes through is exaggerated. But adult baptism still matters, because it makes belonging a commitment instead of a fact imposed at birth.
community-s8d/u9.A: A small percentage of Amish don't become Amish, but a decent majority (like 85% or more) do become Amish because, unlike many other religions, they are not born Amish. They choose it when they become adults. There is some truth to the idea of Rumspringa, but it's probably blown out of proportion in popular media. It's still a pretty big deal that they have to join the church as adults.
community-s8d/u9.B: They do get to choose when they become adults, but it is the choice of an adult, and 85% or more do choose to join the church. The stories about the Rumspringa are exaggerated, and not everyone goes through it. The fact that they are baptized as adults is also very important.

community-s8d/u10.input: Every childhood narrows the future. Most ordinary families don't hand an eighteen-year-old a pile of money to go explore the world. They try to get them ready for some next step that can actually work. A poor or money-free community may have even less cash to offer, and food, medical care and basic survival may rightly come first.
community-s8d/u10.A: That's the thing though, kids born into a culture, that restricts their futures, even if it is a plain boring normal one, are rarely going to be able to just leave. Even in the US, if a kid is born into a normal household, their parents aren't just going to give them a bunch of money and let them go off and see the world when they turn 18. The parents will generally want to see the kids go off and do whatever the next step is for them. If a kid is born into a culture of poor or no money, the parents are often too busy just trying to keep food in their kids mouths and them healthy, to worry about anything else.
community-s8d/u10.B: It depends on the community a kid grew up in, if he or she grew up in a normal community with a normal family. It's unlikely that a family would give their child a bunch of money to go off and see the world at the age of 18, more likely to send them off for whatever comes next. If the kid grew up in a poor, money free community it might not have been able to give him money, and instead had to make sure he had food, medical care and was surviving.

community-s8d/u11.input: The realistic standard isn't unlimited freedom. It's that leaving shouldn't be made artificially impossible. If children grow up without using money, they especially need to know enough about the money world outside not to be helpless in it: jobs, rent, contracts, banking, scams, ID, transportation, and how to ask for help. They need skills and an education they can take with them, relationships outside the community, access to their own records and documents, and at least one plausible next path, whether that's school, an apprenticeship, work, family or another community. If the community can offer temporary housing, help with travel, tools, or a small reserve for the transition, great. If it can't, it can still avoid punishing anyone for leaving, or holding back the knowledge and the records a young adult needs to function somewhere else. No upbringing gives perfect freedom. The point isn't to erase path dependence. It's to not turn belonging into a trap.
community-s8d/u11.A: The realistic standard is not "anything is possible" but rather "it's not impossible". This means that, especially for kids that grew up without money, they should be taught the skills required to survive in the money-world, such as how to find a job, how to pay rent, how to not get scammed, how to deal with the bank, how to get ID, how to travel, how to ask for help etc. This also means that they should be allowed to get the skills and education they need for that, be allowed to make friends outside the community, be allowed to keep records and documents, be allowed to have at least one option for what to do next, and if possible be allowed to have support from the community for the transition (housing, travel, tools etc.). If the community can't allow those things for practical reasons, it should at least not penalise people for leaving and make sure that the above things are not withheld. It's not possible to remove path-dependency, but at least it should be possible to not exploit it.
community-s8d/u11.B: It's not that unrealistic. Not making it artificially impossible for people to leave is a perfectly reasonable standard to have for a community. And for kids especially, even if they grow up without ever using money , they need some education about how the money-world works, and what to do if they need to interact with it. Part of that education is knowing how to get a job, pay rent, sign contracts, open bank accounts, not get scammed, get ID, travel, and how to get help when they need it. It would also be good for them to have transferable skills and education, some friends outside the community, access to their records and documents, and some ideas of where they might go next. The community could also help out with some temporary housing, transportation, tools, etc, if they have the resources. But even if they don't, they can at least not make it harder for people to leave by punishing them for it, or withholding the knowledge or records they need. No upbringing can be completely free, and there will always be some path-dependence, but it doesn't have to be a trap.
